169.title: As the hart panteth (Psalm 41 [42])
169.hook: a deer thirsty for water, and a soul asking why art thou sad
169.carry: why art thou sad, my soul
169.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 41 [42] in the Liturgy of the Hours and hear it at the Easter Vigil when baptisms are celebrated; its Latin, Sicut cervus, has been set to music by many composers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, taste and see, a psalm that became a Communion song. Your line was near to the broken. A new week, and a psalm about thirst.

Late summer, a dry hillside. A deer comes down out of the trees, sides heaving, tongue out, looking for water. The streambed it remembers is cracked mud. It keeps walking, head low, because thirst doesn't let you stop looking. Real thirst, after a long run, a fever, a hot day with no bottle, isn't a thought. It's the whole body wanting one thing. A psalm uses exactly that picture for what it feels like to miss God.
screen: `A DEER ON A DRY HILLSIDE.` → `THE STREAM IS MUD.` → `THIRST ISN'T A THOUGHT.`

segments.voice: Psalm 41 in the Douay, 42 in most Bibles: "As the hart panteth after the fountains of water; so my soul panteth after thee, O God." A hart is a deer. "My soul hath thirsted after the strong living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?" The one praying is far from home, far from the Temple, remembering the days of walking with the festival crowd, singing. Now: "My tears have been my bread day and night, whilst it is said to me daily: Where is thy God?" Tears for bread, and people asking, where's your God now? Then something unusual: the speaker starts talking to their own soul. "Why art thou sad, O my soul? and why dost thou trouble me? Hope in God, for I will still give praise to him." A person arguing gently with their own sadness, not pretending it isn't there, but not letting it run the house either. That refrain comes back three times, across this psalm and the next, which is why some scholars think the two were once a single song. In between, a line about being overwhelmed: "Deep calleth on deep, at the noise of thy flood-gates." Wave after wave rolling over. The Church gives this psalm a place at the Easter Vigil. In the older rite, when there were baptisms, it was sung as the new Christians walked to the font: thirsty deer, going down to the water.

segments.voice: Pour a glass of water, or wait for the next time you drink, and before you drink, notice your thirst, even a little. Drink slowly, feel the water go down, and ask what else you're thirsty for right now, underneath. If you pray, say the psalm's line, my soul hath thirsted after the living God; if you don't, simply notice the thirst and the water meeting.

170.title: Be still (Psalm 45 [46])
170.hook: mountains fall into the sea, and God says be still and see that I am God
170.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 45 [46] in the Liturgy of the Hours and hear it at Mass, including on the feast of the Dedication of the Lateran Basilica, where the river that makes the city of God glad is read alongside images of the Temple.

segments.voice: Yesterday, as the hart panteth: a soul thirsty for God, talking gently to its own sadness. Your line was why art thou sad, my soul. Today, a psalm with an earthquake in it.

The words turn up on mugs and wall prints, in soft script over a calm lake: be still. It looks like a spa slogan. Breathe. Relax. Light a candle. But go back to where the line comes from, and there's no calm lake anywhere. The ground is shaking. Mountains are sliding into the ocean. The sea is roaring. Nations are at war. And right in the middle of all that noise, God speaks.
screen: `A MUG WITH A CALM LAKE.` → `THE REAL SETTING: EARTHQUAKE.` → `GOD SPEAKS IN THE NOISE.`

segments.voice: Psalm 45 in the Douay, 46 in most Bibles, opens: "Our God is our refuge and strength: a helper in troubles, which have found us exceedingly." Troubles that found us, as if they came looking. Then the disaster: "Therefore we will not fear, when the earth shall be troubled; and the mountains shall be removed into the heart of the sea." The solid ground itself gives way. And in the middle of the chaos, a quiet picture: "The stream of the river maketh the city of God joyful." Jerusalem had no great river. The psalm gives it one anyway, a gentle stream that makes a city glad while the sea rages. Then God speaks. He makes wars cease to the ends of the earth, breaks the bow, burns the shields. And then: "Be still and see that I am God." Here's the surprise. The Hebrew word behind be still is usually rendered let go: relax your grip, stop. It's less a spa word than a word you'd shout at two armies: enough, put it down. The Latin Bible put it as vacate: be free, make room. So the line is a command to stop fighting, stop grasping, stop trying to hold the mountains up yourself, and see who God is. In this psalm, stillness isn't what you do once life is calm. It's what you do while it isn't.

segments.voice: For sixty seconds, be still, not calm, just still: let your hands drop into your lap, palms open, as if you've just put something heavy down. Notice what's shaking in your life right now; you don't have to fix any of it for this minute, just stop holding it up. If you pray, hear the line as God's word to you, be still and see that I am God; if you don't, simply let your hands stay open.

171.title: Have mercy on me (Psalm 50 [51])
171.hook: David's psalm after his great sin, prayed every Friday morning
171.howItsDone: Catholics who pray the Liturgy of the Hours say the Miserere every Friday at Morning Prayer; it is one of the seven penitential psalms, and its verse about hyssop gave its name to the Asperges, the sprinkling with holy water.

segments.voice: Yesterday, be still: a command spoken in an earthquake. Your line was be still and see. Today, a psalm of sorrow for sin.

A prophet named Nathan walks into the king's palace with a story. Two men lived in a town, he says. One was rich, with flocks and herds. The other was poor, with one little ewe lamb he raised with his children; it ate from his plate and slept in his arms. When a traveler visited, the rich man spared his own sheep, took the poor man's lamb and served it for dinner. King David is furious. That man deserves to die, he says. And Nathan looks at him and says four words.
screen: `A PROPHET WITH A STORY.` → `THE POOR MAN'S ONE LAMB.` → `DAVID IS FURIOUS.`

segments.voice: "Thou art the man." David had taken another man's wife, Bathsheba, and when she was pregnant, he arranged for her husband Uriah to die in battle. He thought it was hidden. Now it's out. David, a king who could have had the prophet killed, says, "I have sinned against the Lord." The heading of Psalm 50 in the Douay, 51 in most Bibles, ties it to this moment. Its Latin first word names it: Miserere, have mercy. "Have mercy on me, O God, according to thy great mercy." Nothing held back. It asks to be washed: "Thou shalt sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed: thou shalt wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow." Hyssop, a small plant, sprinkled water in purification rites; that verse is why a priest sprinkling holy water over a congregation is traditionally called the Asperges, from its Latin. The center: "Create a clean heart in me, O God: and renew a right spirit within my bowels." Create is the Hebrew verb Genesis opens with, and scholars note the Bible uses it only of God. Not a cleaned-up heart: a new one. Near the end, God doesn't want a burnt offering: "a contrite and humbled heart, O God, thou wilt not despise." The Church prays this psalm every Friday morning in the Liturgy of the Hours, the day Jesus died. It's also behind Allegri's Miserere, said to have been so guarded by the Sistine Chapel that copies were forbidden, until the young Mozart, the story goes, heard it and wrote it down from memory.

segments.voice: Let the psalm's first line be the only thing in your mind, slowly, once on each out-breath: have mercy on me, O God, according to thy great mercy. Don't go looking for your worst sin; let the line find whatever needs it. If you pray, stay with those words to God; if you don't, breathe the word mercy, for yourself and someone you find it hard to forgive.

172.title: My soul thirsteth (Psalm 62 [63])
172.hook: the Sunday morning psalm: early I seek thee in a dry land
172.howItsDone: Catholics who pray the Liturgy of the Hours say Psalm 62 [63] at Morning Prayer on Sundays and on feasts; it has been treated as the Church's morning psalm since at least the fourth century.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Miserere, David's psalm after his great sin. Your line was a clean heart. Today, a morning psalm.

What's the first thing you reach for in the morning? For most people it's the phone, before the eyes are fully open: messages, news, the weather, somebody's vacation photos. The first minute of the day goes to whatever is loudest. An old Christian habit gives that minute to something else. For centuries, monks and nuns greeted the first light with one particular psalm, a song that starts with a person awake early, thirsty, in a dry place.
screen: `THE FIRST THING YOU REACH FOR.` → `THE FIRST MINUTE OF THE DAY.` → `A PSALM BEFORE DAWN.`

segments.voice: Psalm 62 in the Douay, 63 in most Bibles. Its heading places David in the desert, far from the sanctuary. The Douay begins: "O God, my God, to thee do I watch at break of day." The Hebrew verb comes from the word for dawn: I seek you at first light. That's why many English Bibles say early will I seek thee. Then the thirst: my soul thirsts for you, my flesh longs for you, like a dry, weary land where there is no water. Not just the soul; the body too. Then a line that stops people: "For thy mercy is better than lives." Lives, plural. Better than life itself, better than any number of lives. Then the night. If I have remembered you on my bed, the psalm says, I will think of you in the morning. The one praying has been awake in the dark, and wakes still turned toward God. It ends with closeness so physical it's almost a hug: "My soul hath stuck close to thee: thy right hand hath received me." Clinging, the way a child holds a parent's leg. Saint John Chrysostom, in the fourth century, said the fathers before him had appointed it to be sung every morning. Today in the Liturgy of the Hours it opens Morning Prayer on Sundays and on great feasts. The first minute of the day, given to thirst.
screen: `TO THEE DO I WATCH AT BREAK OF DAY.` · `A DRY LAND WITH NO WATER.` · `THY MERCY IS BETTER THAN LIVES.` · `MY SOUL HATH STUCK CLOSE TO THEE.`

segments.voice: Picture the moment you wake, eyes still heavy, the phone somewhere nearby, and before you touch it, one line: O God, my God, to thee do I watch at break of day. Say it now, three times, slowly, so it's ready for the morning. If you pray, let it be your first word to God tomorrow; if you don't, let it be a way of choosing what gets your first minute.

173.title: How lovely are thy tabernacles (Psalm 83 [84])
173.hook: even the sparrow finds a home near the altar
173.tomorrow: Teach us to number our days (Psalm 89 [90])
173.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 83 [84] in the Liturgy of the Hours and hear it at Mass, often on feasts of dedication of churches; some also make short visits to a church simply to sit in the quiet.

segments.voice: Yesterday, my soul thirsteth: shachar, dawn, and the morning psalm. Your line was early I seek you. Today, a psalm about a place.

A weekday afternoon in an old stone church, and something is moving near the ceiling. A sparrow flew in through an open door and now lives in the rafters, hopping along a beam above the altar, unbothered by the saints and the candles. People smile at it. The sexton sighs about it. Long ago, a pilgrim walking into the Temple in Jerusalem noticed the same thing, a small bird nesting near the altar, and felt a stab of envy.
screen: `AN OLD STONE CHURCH.` → `A SPARROW IN THE RAFTERS.` → `A PILGRIM'S ENVY.`

segments.voice: Psalm 83 in the Douay, 84 in most Bibles, is a pilgrim's song: "How lovely are thy tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! my soul longeth and fainteth for the courts of the Lord." Tabernacles here means dwellings, the courts of the Temple. Fainteth: homesick to the point of weakness. Then the bird. "For the sparrow hath found herself a house, and the turtle a nest for herself where she may lay her young ones: Thy altars, O Lord of hosts." The turtle is a turtledove. Two small, ordinary birds get to live at the altar full time, while the pilgrim can only visit. It's funny and aching at once. Then the road. Blessed are those whose strength is in you, the psalm says, who have set their hearts on the journey, and it names a valley they pass through. The Hebrew calls it the valley of Baca, a place scholars can't pin down. The name may mean balsam trees, or weeping. The Latin read it as weeping, so the Douay says: "In the vale of tears." Tradition traces the phrase vale of tears to this verse; it's the same valley of tears the Hail, Holy Queen sighs through. In the Hebrew, the pilgrims pass through it and make it a place of springs. Then the famous line: "For better is one day in thy courts above thousands." One day near God, better than a thousand anywhere else. Centuries later, Brahms set its opening lines in his German Requiem.
screen: `MY SOUL LONGETH AND FAINTETH.` · `THE SPARROW FOUND A HOUSE.` · `THROUGH THE VALE OF TEARS.` · `ONE DAY ABOVE THOUSANDS.`

segments.voice: Sit somewhere quiet, a church if one is near, or the quietest corner you can find, even a parked car, and picture the sparrow on the beam, completely at home. Ask yourself where you feel that at home, and when you last were there. If you pray, say how lovely are thy tabernacles, O Lord; if you don't, let this quiet corner be a small place to rest.
Tabernacles. Dwellings, the courts of the Temple, the pilgrim's homesick song for God's house, where even the sparrow has a home. Today's word.

174.title: Teach us to number our days (Psalm 89 [90])
174.word: Teach us to number our days
174.hook: a thousand years are as yesterday to God
174.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 89 [90] in the Liturgy of the Hours and hear it at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time, when the readings turn to the shortness of life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, how lovely are thy tabernacles, and a sparrow at home near the altar. Your line was the sparrow found a home. Today, a psalm about time.

Time is strange. A bad afternoon at the dentist lasts forever. A whole summer vanishes. A photo from ten years ago feels like last month. Next week's calendar is already full. Then comes the moment of looking up and asking: where did it all go? The oldest voice in the whole psalter, by tradition, asked the same thing, and asked God to teach him what to do about it.
screen: `AN AFTERNOON LASTS FOREVER.` → `A SUMMER VANISHES.` → `WHERE DID IT GO?`

segments.voice: Psalm 89 in the Douay, 90 in most Bibles, carries the heading a prayer of Moses, the man of God. It starts with God's time: "Lord, thou hast been our refuge from generation to generation." Before the mountains were born, before the earth was formed, from eternity to eternity, you are God. Then our time: "For a thousand years in thy sight are as yesterday, which is past. And as a watch in the night." A watch was a shift of guard duty, a few hours. A thousand years, to God, is one night shift. The New Testament echoes it: "one day with the Lord is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day." And human life? Like grass: in the morning it springs up and flowers; by evening it's cut down and dry. Our years are seventy, the psalm says, or eighty if we're strong, and they're gone quickly, and we fly away. It's a hard, honest psalm. Then the line in today's title, the way the Hebrew and the King James have it: teach us to number our days, that we may get a heart of wisdom. Counting the days isn't morbid here. It's the road to a wise heart. A surprise for Douay readers: the old Latin, and the Douay after it, read that verse quite differently, as a prayer that God make his right hand known, and hearts be taught in wisdom. Same hope, different road. The psalm ends asking God to satisfy us in the morning with mercy, and to establish the work of our hands.
screen: `A PRAYER OF MOSES.` · `A THOUSAND YEARS, ONE NIGHT SHIFT.` · `LIKE GRASS BY EVENING.` · `NUMBER OUR DAYS, GET WISDOM.`

segments.voice: Look at the time and work out roughly how many waking hours you have left today: four, nine? Hold that number with attention, not panic, and ask what one thing you'd most want those hours to hold: a conversation, a task, rest, kindness. If you pray, ask as the psalm does, teach me to number my days; if you don't, let the number sharpen what matters.
Teach us to number our days. The prayer of Moses: our time is short, so let counting it make us wise. Today's word.

175.title: He that dwelleth (Psalm 90 [91])
175.hook: under his wings, and angels to keep thee in all thy ways
175.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 90 [91] at Night Prayer on Sundays and on the first Sunday of Lent, when the Gospel tells of the temptation in the desert; some pray daily to their guardian angel, and the Church keeps the feast of the Guardian Angels on October 2.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a prayer of Moses: teach us to number our days. Your line was number your days. Today closes the week, under wings.

If you grew up Catholic, there may have been a small picture over your bed: two children crossing a rickety bridge over a gorge at night, planks broken, water rushing below, and behind them, huge and gentle, an angel with its wings spread, keeping them from falling. Sentimental, maybe. But the idea behind it is old and serious, and a lot of it comes from one psalm, a psalm the devil himself once quoted.
screen: `TWO CHILDREN ON A BROKEN BRIDGE.` → `AN ANGEL BEHIND THEM.` → `A PSALM THE DEVIL QUOTED.`

segments.voice: Psalm 90 in the Douay, 91 in most Bibles: "He that dwelleth in the aid of the most High, shall abide under the protection of the God of Jacob." Then a mother bird: "He will overshadow thee with his shoulders: and under his wings thou shalt trust." Then the fears: the terror of the night, the arrow that flies by day, the thing that walks about in the dark, the noonday devil. And then: "For he hath given his angels charge over thee; to keep thee in all thy ways. In their hands they shall bear thee up: lest thou dash thy foot against a stone." Here's where the devil comes in. In the desert, Matthew says, the tempter took Jesus to the top of the Temple, quoted these lines, and said: jump. The angels will catch you. Scripture, used as bait. Jesus answered with other scripture: "Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God." The psalm is a promise of care, not a dare. From this psalm, and from Jesus's words that children's angels always see the face of his Father in heaven, the Church draws its teaching on guardian angels. The Catechism says that beside each believer stands an angel as protector and shepherd, and that human life, from its beginning until death, is surrounded by the angels' care. Catholics keep a feast of the guardian angels on October 2, and there's a short traditional prayer to one's angel, the kind children learn by heart. It's also the Church's Sunday night psalm, at Compline. The week ran from a thirsty deer to be still, a clean heart, a morning thirst, a sparrow's home and numbered days, and ends here: under his wings.
screen: `UNDER HIS WINGS THOU SHALT TRUST.` · `ANGELS TO KEEP THEE.` · `THE DEVIL QUOTES IT: JUMP.` · `A GUARDIAN FROM CHILDHOOD.`

segments.voice: Think of your own rickety bridge this week, whatever feels unsteady, and something large and gentle behind you, wings open, not stopping you from walking, just keeping you from falling. If you pray, speak to your guardian angel in your own words, or with the traditional prayer to the guardian angel; if you don't, rest in the picture of being kept.
Guardian angel. The angel Catholics believe stands beside each believer, as protector and shepherd, from the beginning of life until death. Today's word.
